steps.hints: ❓Did you set the <is button pressed> value blocks to the correct direction to match the [set sprite image to] blocks?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solutions:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions is the Player sprite able to move in?

❓ Why is it even more important that the sprite image matches the direction they are moving in a 2D platformer project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to connect the vx/vy values in the [move sprite with buttons] block to how they set a sprite’s velocity y in the previous activities. Remind the ninja that x values determine the left/right direction of a sprite, whereas y values determine the up/down direction. 

💡 Because the 2D platformer shows a side-view, setting the sprite image to match the direction that the sprite is moving in improves the game player’s experience.
steps.instructions:
Set the Player sprite to move left and right across the tilemap!


Drag a [move sprite with buttons] block into the [on start] container. Select the Player sprite’s name, then click + to show the block’s parameters. Change vy to “0” so the sprite can only move left and right.


Drag two <is button pressed> value blocks into the < > openings of the conditional inside the [forever] loop. Click the drop down and select [left] or [right] to match the direction the [set sprite image to] block shows.


Click ▶ to move the Player sprite left and right and notice if it is facing the correct direction as it moves.

steps.hints: ❓Did you set the Player sprite’s velocity y and acceleration y so it jumps when the A button is pressed, and then falls back to the ground?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What happens when the A button is pressed? Does the car sprite move as you expected it would? 

❓ Is the Player sprite able to jump high enough onto the platform to avoid the lava?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to practice moving the Player sprite and jumping onto each of the platforms. Is there a certain strategy that’s more helpful? Are there any parts of the tilemap that they are unable to reach?
steps.instructions:
Code the Player sprite to jump onto the platform to avoid the lava!


Drag out an [on button pressed] container. Open Sprites and drag a [set sprite [x]] block into the container. Click the drop down and select [vy (velocity y)] then set the parameter to -250. This will allow the sprite to move up when the A button is pressed.


Drag another [set sprite [x]] block into the [on start] container below the Player sprite’s blocks. Click the drop down and select [ay (acceleration y)], then set the parameter to 600. This will create “gravity” that pulls the sprite back to the ground.


Click ▶ then press the A button to make the Player sprite jump onto the platform to avoid the lava.

steps.hints: ❓Did you replace the <true> value of the [if then] conditional with an <is sprite hitting wall> and select [bottom] from the drop down?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ Is the Player sprite able to jump while it’s in the air? Why or why not?

❓ Why would you want the Player sprite to be able to jump only when on a wall tile?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Prompt the ninja to think about what happens when they try to jump in the air in real life—are they able to jump when not standing on a solid surface? Encourage the ninja to consider why they would want to add this realistic element to a game.
steps.instructions:
Prevent the Player sprite from flying through the air!


To code the Player sprite to jump only when the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall, drag an [if then] conditional into the [on A button pressed] container then drag the [set sprite vy (velocity y)] block into it. 


Open Scene then drag an <is sprite hitting wall> value block into the <true> value of the conditional. Select the Player sprite’s name, then select [bottom] from the drop down.


Click ▶ then press the A button to test when the sprite is able to jump.

steps.hints: ❓Did you edit the tilemap and use the Draw Walls icon to set platform tiles as walls?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you add walls to tiles on the tilemap? 

❓ Why should the floor and platform tiles act as walls in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Point out to the ninja that walls and platforms should be consistent, so that the user knows what to expect. If a tile looks the same, such as the floor and platform tiles, then they should act the same (both as walls).

💡Make sure the Ninja uses the provided tilemap and only adds walls to the existing  floor and platform tiles. They should not add any other customizations to the tilemap; those can be added once saved to My Stuff.
steps.instructions:
Oh no! The Player sprite is able to jump through the other floors and platforms!


To make the floor and platform tiles “walls”, click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to open the tilemap editor. Click on the “Draw Walls” icon then paint or fill the remaining floor and platform tiles so they become walls.


Click ▶ then move the Player sprite around the tilemap to test if the floor and platforms are now acting as walls.

steps.hints: ❓Did you select the yellow tile in the (array of all tile locations) block?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How does the project know how many and where to place the Food sprites?

❓ Is the Player sprite able to reach the Food sprites by jumping?

❓ How else might collectible and obstacle sprites be used in this project?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Walk the ninja through the sequence of the [for element] loop. In this example, for each yellow spawn tile on the tilemap, the project will place a star sprite on top of it and then make the tile blank. Because it uses the array of all yellow spawn tiles, the project knows how many tiles are in the array and where they are each located on the tilemap.
steps.instructions:
Add Food sprites for the Player sprite to jump up and collect!


Drag a [for element] loop into the bottom of the [on start] container, then drag the Food sprite’s code blocks inside. 


Open Scene, then drag an (array of all tile locations) block into the (list) value in the loop. Select the yellow tile from the drop down. The yellow tile is a spawn tile and is setting the place for Food sprites to be created.


Open Scene, then drag [place sprite on top of tile] and [set tile at] blocks into the loop. Update the Food sprite’s name, then replace the tilemap coordinates in both blocks with the (value) variable from the loop. Leave the tile blank in the [set tile at] block.


Click ▶ to see the Food sprites appear in place of the 2 yellow spawn tiles.

steps.hints: ❓Did you edit the tilemap to include more yellow spawn tiles that will turn into Food sprites?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How do you add new tiles to the tilemap?

❓ Where should the Food sprites be placed on the tilemap, so that they are challenging but not impossible for the Player sprite to reach?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think strategically about where they want to place the yellow spawn tiles/star sprites. Prompt them to think about whether they should be above a platform, in open space, or near a lava tile.
steps.instructions:
Add more Food sprites for the Player sprite to jump up and collect!


To add at least 4 more Food sprites to the game, click the square in the [set tilemap to] block to open the tilemap editor.


Select “My Tiles” then select the yellow tile. Click on the tilemap to draw at least 4 more yellow spawn tiles that will turn into Food sprites for the Player sprite to collect.


Click ▶ to see all of the yellow spawn tiles turn into Food sprites!

steps.hints: ❓Did you add a dialog box in both conditions so that players know what to do when they overlap the magic portal tile?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ How many star sprites are located on the tilemap? How many star sprites should the Player sprite need to collect?

❓ What kind of message should be added to the conditional to tell the Player sprite whether the magic portal is open or not?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡 Encourage the ninja to think about what value the Player sprite should aim to reach for the score to end. If there are 5 star sprites on the screen, should they win if they collect 3 sprites? 4 sprites? 5 sprites?
steps.instructions:
Open the magic portal door when the Player sprite collects enough Food sprites!


Drag out an [on sprite overlaps tile] container, select the magic portal tile as the parameter, then drag an [if then else] conditional inside. Use a <0=0> comparison block to test if the (score) is greater than or equal to (≥) a certain number of stars.


If the (score) is greater than or equal to (≥) the number of Food sprites, a dialog box should announce that the portal has opened, and the game should end in a “win”. Else, a dialog box should tell the Player sprite to go back and collect more stars, then return the Player sprite to its starting position.


Click ▶ to see what happens when the Player sprite touches the magic portal door!

steps.hints: ❓ Did you add customizations to your project, such as dialog boxes, splash screens, or effects?
steps.senseiHelp:
Solution:

Ask the ninja:

❓ What directions might help a user understand how to play the game?


Sensei Pro Tip:

💡Guide ninjas to note that while these customizing blocks are open ended and not required for the game to “work”, they really improve the Player’s experience playing a game, either by giving context to what the Player should do or not do, or to provide a more fun experience overall. They also allow the Ninja to add their personal touch and express themselves through small details present in the game.
steps.instructions:
Add a dialog box at the beginning of the game to provide instructions to the user. Customize the dialog box with a frame, too!


Click ▶ to play the finished game!

subgroups.introduction: Create a 2D platformer project where a Player sprite must jump up onto platforms to avoid lava tiles and collect stars to open a secret portal door!

validationItems.text: Player sprite moves left and right across the tilemap, facing the direction it is moving in.
Player sprite can only jump up when the bottom of the sprite is touching a tilemap wall tile.
Set tilemap floor and platform tiles as walls.
Spawn Food sprites to appear on the tilemap.
Add additional spawn tiles to the tilemap.
Magic Portal tile shares feedback and ends the game when the Player sprite earns enough points.
Game instructions and specific feedback, depending on score conditions, are shared in dialog boxes.

attributes.description: Welcome to Level 1 of Green Belt! In this level, you’ll learn more about 2D platformer games and physics. In 2D platformers, we see the game as if looking from the side. We can use physics concepts, like velocity and acceleration, to make our sprites jump up onto platforms and avoid obstacles. Here are the achievements you’ll unlock in Level 1:

badges.title: Let’s Get Physics-cal!
badges.description: Use physics to control sprite movement in a platformer-style tilemap project.

badges.title: Hop, Skip, and a Jump
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-velocity (vy).

badges.title: Defying Gravity
badges.description: Set a sprite’s y-acceleration (ay).

badges.title: Wallflower
badges.description: Check if a sprite is touching a tilemap wall before making something happen in a project.
